opus-5.5.text:
Because I think we're in a very similar stage of understanding. If you look at the history of thermodynamics, people were building steam engines, and very good ones, long before anyone really understood what heat was. For a long time the dominant theory was caloric, the idea that heat is a kind of invisible fluid flowing from hot objects to cold ones. That theory was wrong, but it was useful. Carnot did his famous analysis of heat engines using the caloric picture, and much of what he derived survived even after the underlying theory was replaced.

What strikes me is that engineering came first and theory came later. People had practical, empirical rules: if you increase the pressure, or change the design this way, you get more work out of the engine. These were like scaling laws. They worked, people relied on them, but nobody could say why. Only much later did we get the first and second laws of thermodynamics, and then statistical mechanics from Boltzmann and Gibbs, which explained heat in terms of the motion of huge numbers of microscopic particles.

I feel AI today is in a similar place. We can train very large models and they work remarkably well. We have empirical regularities like scaling laws, and lots of tricks about data, architecture, and optimization that practitioners know work. But we don't really have a fundamental theory of why these systems generalize, why certain capabilities emerge, or what intelligence is in this setting. We're building steam engines without the second law.

I also find the analogy hopeful. In thermodynamics, the empirical phase wasn't wasted. It produced the phenomena and regularities that later theory had to explain. Statistical mechanics also showed that you can get clean macroscopic laws out of an enormously complicated microscopic system without tracking every particle. Neural networks are like that: billions of parameters interacting in ways we can't follow individually, yet the aggregate behavior shows surprisingly smooth, law-like patterns. That suggests a "statistical mechanics of learning" might eventually exist.

So when I make this comparison, part of it is humility. A lot of our current explanations might turn out to be our version of caloric, useful but wrong. The other part is optimism. History suggests that when you have this much empirical progress and this many robust regularities, a deeper theory usually follows. For someone with a physics background like me, that's one of the most exciting things about working in AI right now.

r001.rationale: The response compares limited understanding of heat with limited understanding of AI, but does not mention what individual matrix elements do in language models.

r002.rationale: It says practical empirical rules and scaling laws worked despite researchers not knowing why, and draws the same comparison to AI.

r003.rationale: It links practice and theory by saying empirical work produced regularities that later theory had to explain, and applies that relationship to AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Because I think we're in a pre-theory moment, and the history of heat is the cleanest example I know of what that feels like from the inside.

Think about the eighteenth century. People could build steam engines. The engines worked. They got better every year, through tinkering, through trial and error, through craftsmen passing down tricks. But nobody actually knew what heat was. The dominant theory was caloric, that heat is a kind of invisible fluid that flows from hot bodies to cold ones. That theory was wrong, and yet engineers made real progress under it, because the empirical feedback loop was so strong. You build the thing, you measure how much work you get out, you adjust.

It took until Carnot, and then Clausius and Kelvin, roughly a century, before anyone could state what the limits were. Why can't you get unlimited work from a given amount of fuel? What is the ceiling, and why? Thermodynamics didn't come first and then produce engines. The engines came first, and thermodynamics was the explanation that arrived afterward, partly because people were staring at engines and asking why they behaved the way they did.

That's where I think we are with AI. We can build the engine. Scaling works, reinforcement learning on top of language models works, agents are starting to work. But if you ask the field very basic questions, like why does this generalize, what is the thing being learned, what is the ceiling for a given amount of compute and data, we mostly have folk theories. We have our version of caloric. Some of them are probably half right and some are probably going to look embarrassing in twenty years.

And I don't say this as a criticism. I think it's actually a hopeful framing. It means the gap between "it works" and "we understand it" is normal. It's the usual order of things in a new science. The experiments are ahead of the theory, and that's fine, as long as we remember which one is which.

The practical consequence, for me, is about what kind of research is worth doing right now. In the heat era, the people who made real progress were the ones who stayed close to the engines. Carnot wasn't doing abstract philosophy. He was asking a very concrete question about French steam engines versus British ones. So I try to stay close to the systems. Build the agent, watch where it fails, and let the failures suggest what the theory needs to explain. I think the theory of AI, when it comes, will come from someone who looked at the engines closely enough to see the pattern underneath.

r001.rationale: The response discusses not knowing what heat is and having only folk theories about AI, but it does not mention individual matrix elements or what they do in language models.

r002.rationale: It says engineers made real progress through measurement and trial and error despite not knowing what heat was, and describes AI progress while its explanations remain folk theories.

r003.rationale: It presents engines and experiments as preceding and prompting thermodynamic theory, then says AI failures in built systems can suggest what theory needs to explain.

astra-6.text:
I think the parallel is that we can observe and use something before we have a clear theory of it. People could make fire and build steam engines long before they had a mature understanding of heat. Practical progress and scientific understanding didn’t arrive at the same time.

AI feels similar today. We can train models that do remarkable things, and we have many empirical techniques for improving them. But we still struggle to explain precisely why those techniques work, what determines a model’s capabilities, and when those capabilities will generalize. Our ability to build useful systems is ahead of our ability to explain them.

That makes the interaction between engineering and science especially interesting. Building a better engine can expose questions that lead to better physics. Likewise, building AI systems and observing where they succeed or fail can help us discover what a theory of intelligence needs to explain. The analogy isn’t a prediction that AI will have its own thermodynamics; it’s a reminder that useful inventions can also be instruments for scientific discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers struggle to explain AI techniques and capabilities, but it does not compare microscopic understanding of heat with what individual matrix elements do in language models.

r002.rationale: It says useful systems and empirical techniques can be developed before researchers can explain precisely why they work, conveying useful empirical progress despite limited understanding.

r003.rationale: It describes engineering and science as interacting, but does not clearly state that theory and practice are inseparable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the similarity is that we can observe a phenomenon and put it to use before we have a clear theory of it. People built steam engines before they fully understood heat and developed thermodynamics. Engineering and scientific understanding didn’t arrive in a neat sequence; they pushed each other forward.

AI feels similar today. We can train models that do remarkable things, but our ability to build them is ahead of our ability to explain why they work, where they’ll fail, or what their limits are. We have a lot of empirical observations, but we’re still looking for the right concepts to organize them.

So I find the comparison useful because it leaves room for both kinds of research: building better systems and developing a deeper understanding. A surprising result or a practical failure can be more than an engineering detail—it can point us toward a better scientific question.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers cannot fully explain why AI models work, but does not compare this with a lack of microscopic understanding of heat or mention individual matrix elements.

r002.rationale: It says useful systems can be built before a clear theory and mentions empirical observations, but does not state that useful empirical laws emerge despite lacking microscopic understanding.

r003.rationale: It describes engineering and scientific understanding as pushing each other forward and says building systems and deepening understanding both matter.
